To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the sense of agency is based on the integration of different sources of information, including the internal motor command and external sensory feedback, and that this integration is reflected in different neural signatures.

(i) self-generated and external errors show distinct neural signatures; (ii) these signatures are different in terms of latency, scalp topography and amplitude; (iii) the violation of the sense-of-agency elicited by externally generated errors is associated with a neural signature that resembles the N400, which is usually related to semantic violations.

(1) self-generated and externally generated errors elicit different ERP components; (2) the violation of the sense agency is associated to the same ERP component (N400) that has been associated to semantic violations; (3) this component is only observed when participants are the agents of the movements.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of how we can recognize ourselves as the agent of our own actions, in other words: how do we know that a particular action is self-generated or externally imposed?
how we recognize ourselves as actors and agents of our actions.
the question of how we can recognize ourselves as agents of our actions.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
we have two distinct error-monitoring mechanisms, one for self-generated errors (Ne/ERN) and one for externally-generated errors (N400) that are both involved in the process of action recognition.
the N400 component elicited by the violation of the sense-of-agency is a specific neural signature of the detection of the violation of the body movement semantic.
we are not only able to detect errors in our actions, but also able to detect errors that are not our own.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have identified two different neural signatures for self-generated and external errors, and that these signatures are differentially modulated by the presence of a self-representation.
the human brain has two different error detection systems, one for monitoring our own actions, and another one for monitoring external actions.
we found that there is a difference between the brain responses for the self-generated and externally-generated errors.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the sense of agency, i.e., our ability to recognize ourselves as the originator of our own actions, is a fundamental aspect of our conscious experience.
the brain is equipped with two different error monitoring mechanisms, which can be activated in parallel, and which are sensitive to the origin of the error (self-generated vs. externally-generated).
the brain has a very specific neural signature to identify the errors we commit and those that are imposed by the environment, which is not shared with the detection of semantic violations.
